questions.modelAnswer: [From the text, page 339] Canadians realize the positive benefits of immigration including economic development and the creation of jobs for native-born Canadians. This is because a large proportion of Canadian immigrants are highly skilled people who are net contributors to the economy. Also, with a sparse population and low birth rate, Canada needs immigrants for population growth and economic development. About two-thirds of Canada’s permanent visas are granted for Canada’s economic needs, including the filling of labor shortages; in contrast, about two-thirds of U.S. green cards are granted for family reunions. Canadians consider multiculturalism as a key ingredient of their national identity. They contend that people who are exposed to different viewpoints and cultures are more likely to cooperate with one another or reach a compromise when differences occur and become more productive by learning from others. Canadians generally see immigration as adding to the social fabric of the country. Finally, Canada has little reason to fear illegal immigration. Although Canada and the United States share a long border, millions of Americans do not wish to move to Canada. In other words, the United States serves as a buffer zone for unauthorized immigration that reduces Canadian anxiety about it. Canada emphasizes open immigration policies that accept talented foreigners who have the skills the country needs and the desire to succeed. Canada has transformed itself into an immigrant country, with a foreign-born population (20 percent) exceeding that of the United States (13 percent). Most Canadians feel that this infusion of talent has added to the economic vitality of Canada.

questions.prompt: What particular aspects of multinational operations generate potential conflict?
options: Employment, technology transfer, national sovereignty, balance of payments, transfer pricing, and taxes can generate conflicts.
Only the physical color of a foreign firm’s products can cause conflict.
Intrafirm transactions make tax and sovereignty concerns impossible.
MNE operations eliminate all disagreements between host and source countries.
questions.explanation: Answers should focus on issues such as employment impacts, technology transfer, national sovereignty, balance-of-payments, transfer pricing, and tax policy. Answers could also include negative net welfare impacts of joint ventures.
questions.modelAnswer: Answers should focus on issues such as employment impacts, technology transfer, national sovereignty, balance-of-payments, transfer pricing, and tax policy. Answers could also include negative net welfare impacts of joint ventures.

questions.prompt: What does the inward spiral in the historical trade chart indicate?
options: World trade contracted over the years shown.
questions.explanation: Points closer to the center represent smaller trade values. The spiral moves inward from 1929 toward 1933.
questions.topic: Protectionism and the collapse of trade

questions.prompt: What is plotted along the spokes of the chart?
questions.explanation: The spokes are labeled with calendar months; the nested paths allow comparisons across years.
questions.topic: Protectionism and the collapse of trade

questions.prompt: Can this chart alone establish how much of the trade collapse was caused by tariffs?
options: No; it does not isolate tariffs from other causes.
Yes; all of the collapse is necessarily caused by tariffs.
Yes; it proves tariffs had no effect.
No; it contains no time information.
questions.explanation: A historical chart shows changes, not an experiment holding the Depression and other influences constant.
questions.topic: Protectionism and the collapse of trade

questions.prompt: Which policy response can amplify the contraction associated with a tariff increase?
options: Trading partners retaliate with their own trade barriers.
All partners permanently eliminate their tariffs.
All domestic firms gain foreign market access.
questions.explanation: Retaliation reduces export opportunities and can compound restrictions on international trade.
questions.topic: Protectionism and the collapse of trade

questions.prompt: Which measurement concern matters when interpreting a chart of trade in dollars?
options: Dollar trade values can fall because prices fall, quantities fall, or both.
Dollar values measure physical quantities without any price influence.
Dollar values always measure welfare directly.
A price decline must increase the dollar value of trade.
questions.explanation: Value equals price times quantity. A value chart does not by itself separate these components.
questions.topic: Protectionism and the collapse of trade

questions.prompt: Which statement best connects the chart to the lecture’s policy history?
options: The protectionist episode helps explain the later shift toward reciprocal trade liberalization.
The chart proves all subsequent trade agreements abolished tariffs immediately.
The chart shows the WTO existed in 1930.
The chart measures a loan guarantee.
questions.explanation: The lecture connects the protectionist period to the Reciprocal Trade Agreements Act and later cooperative trade policy.
questions.topic: Protectionism and the collapse of trade

questions.prompt: In the steel-market panel, what is the immediate effect of a lower price for imported steel?
options: Domestic buyers pay less and domestic steel producers face more competition.
questions.explanation: Cheaper imports benefit steel users while putting pressure on competing domestic producers.

questions.prompt: Who is upstream from steel producers in the lecture’s example?
questions.explanation: Upstream industries supply inputs to the industry being studied; ore is an input into steel.

questions.prompt: Who is downstream from steel producers in the example?
questions.explanation: Downstream firms use steel as an input. Cheaper steel can lower their production costs.

questions.prompt: What does an effective countervailing duty tend to do to the domestic price of subsidized imported steel?
options: Raise it toward the price without the foreign subsidy.
questions.explanation: A countervailing duty offsets the foreign subsidy’s price advantage rather than subsidizing buyers further.

questions.prompt: Why can a duty that helps domestic steel producers hurt domestic car makers?
options: It raises the price of a major input for car makers.
It gives car makers free steel.
It eliminates every foreign car producer.
It raises steel quality by definition.
questions.explanation: The same price rise that protects steel producers raises costs for firms that use steel.

questions.prompt: Which claim is justified by the three linked panels?
options: Protection can create gains and losses in different domestic industries.
Protection necessarily benefits every domestic industry.
Consumer gains always equal national losses.
Upstream and downstream industries respond identically.
questions.explanation: Follow the input chain. Effects on one protected industry are not the same as the effects on the whole economy.

questions.prompt: In the loan-guarantee diagram, which curve changes when the guarantee is introduced?
options: The supply of loanable funds shifts outward.
questions.explanation: Reducing lenders’ risk makes them willing to supply more funds at a given interest rate.

questions.prompt: What happens to the equilibrium interest rate in the slide?
questions.explanation: The vertical axis measures interest rates. The new intersection is at 4%, below the original 6%.

questions.prompt: By how much does the equilibrium quantity of loans rise?
questions.explanation: Loans rise from $20 million to $30 million. The increase is 30 minus 20, or $10 million.

questions.prompt: What is the percentage increase in the quantity of loans?
questions.explanation: The increase is $10 million relative to the original $20 million: 10 / 20 × 100 = 50%.

questions.prompt: How large is the fall in the interest rate in percentage points?
questions.explanation: Subtract the rates: 6% minus 4% equals 2 percentage points. The relative percentage decline is a different calculation.

questions.prompt: Does increased lending prove the guarantee has no cost to taxpayers?
options: No; a guarantee can expose the government to losses if borrowers default.
Yes; every loan guarantee is costless.
Yes; supply shifts cannot have fiscal effects.
No; the entire loan amount is automatically a certain loss.
questions.explanation: A guarantee transfers some default risk. Its expected fiscal cost is not necessarily zero or the full face value of the loans.

questions.prompt: How should you find Airbus’s best response to Boeing producing?
options: Hold Boeing’s action fixed and compare Airbus’s payoffs from producing and not producing.
Add every payoff in the whole table.
Choose the cell with the most text.
questions.explanation: A best response is the action that gives one firm its highest payoff for a given action by its rival.

questions.prompt: What is the intended effect of the European subsidy in this matrix?
options: Make Airbus production more attractive and potentially shift profits toward Airbus.
Eliminate every fixed cost for Boeing.
Force consumers to buy no aircraft.
Make aircraft production perfectly competitive by definition.
questions.explanation: Strategic support changes the supported firm’s payoff and may change the rival’s entry or production decision.

questions.prompt: Why can a firm prefer not to produce when its rival is already producing?
options: Producing may generate a loss when both firms compete for a limited market.
Not producing always creates infinite revenue.
All aircraft markets have zero fixed costs.
Firms ignore profit in payoff matrices.
questions.explanation: Large fixed costs and divided sales can make simultaneous production unprofitable.

questions.prompt: What is a Nash equilibrium in this setting?
options: A pair of actions where neither firm benefits by changing its own action alone.
The cell with the largest sum of revenue regardless of individual incentives.
Any cell selected by the government.
A situation where the two firms must have equal profits.
questions.explanation: Check each firm’s best response while keeping the other firm’s action fixed.

questions.prompt: Why is Airbus’s profit after a subsidy not automatically Europe’s net welfare gain?
options: The public cost of the subsidy must also be considered.
Profits are never part of national welfare.
Boeing’s revenue must always be counted as European income.
Government spending has no opportunity cost.
questions.explanation: The firm can gain partly from a transfer funded by taxpayers. Net national gains require subtracting real public costs.

questions.prompt: Which limitation makes this policy risky in practice?
options: Governments may misjudge costs and demand, and trading partners may retaliate.
Governments always know every firm’s exact future profit.
Foreign governments are unable to respond.
questions.explanation: The lecture emphasizes information problems, special interests, and retaliation as limits to strategic trade policy.

questions.prompt: For a given demand shift, when is the price change generally larger?
options: When the supply curve is horizontal.
When producers can expand output without limit at the old price.
questions.explanation: Less elastic means quantity supplied changes less in response to price. More of the adjustment occurs through price.

questions.prompt: For a given supply shift, when is the price change generally larger?
options: When buyers absorb any extra quantity at the old price.
questions.explanation: Inelastic buyers change quantity little, so a supply change produces a relatively large price movement.

questions.prompt: If crop supply expands while demand is inelastic, what can happen to farmers’ total revenue?
options: Revenue can fall despite a larger quantity sold.
Revenue must rise by the same percentage as quantity.
questions.explanation: With inelastic demand, the percentage price decline can exceed the percentage increase in quantity, reducing price times quantity.

questions.prompt: What does export revenue equal in this simple market?
options: Export price multiplied by quantity exported.
questions.explanation: Revenue is what sellers receive: the price of each unit times the number of units sold.

questions.prompt: Which structural feature makes a developing economy more exposed to this instability?
options: Heavy dependence on a few primary commodity exports.
Perfect diversification across unrelated income sources.
questions.explanation: A concentrated export base makes changes in a single commodity market more important for national export income.

questions.prompt: Why is primary-product supply often inelastic in the short run?
options: Production takes time to adjust, as with growing a crop or developing a mine.
Producers can instantly create unlimited output.
Every commodity has an infinite inventory.
questions.explanation: Biological and investment lags limit short-run quantity responses, so shocks can produce large price movements.

questions.prompt: At a defended price ceiling, demand exceeds current production. What should the buffer-stock manager do?
options: Sell stored stocks to cover the shortage.
Buy more of the current output.
questions.explanation: Selling adds supply to the market and prevents the shortage from pushing the price above the ceiling.

questions.prompt: At a defended price floor, production exceeds demand. What should the manager do?
options: Cut the target price to zero automatically.
Require consumers to reduce purchases further.
questions.explanation: Buying removes surplus output from the market and supports the floor price.

questions.prompt: At a target price, quantity demanded is 80 and quantity supplied is 50. How much must be sold from stocks?
questions.explanation: The shortage is demand minus supply: 80 − 50 = 30. These are illustrative quantities for the same mechanism.

questions.prompt: At a target price, quantity supplied is 90 and quantity demanded is 60. How much must the manager buy?
questions.explanation: The surplus is supply minus demand: 90 − 60 = 30. Buying it prevents downward pressure on the defended price.

questions.prompt: Which constraint can prevent the manager from defending a price ceiling?
options: Running out of stored stocks to sell.
Holding too much cash to buy stocks.
A surplus of current production at the ceiling.
An unlimited reserve of the commodity.
questions.explanation: A ceiling defense during a shortage requires physical inventory. Finite reserves can be exhausted.

questions.prompt: Suppose the manager buys 30 units at $5 each. What is the immediate purchase expenditure?
questions.explanation: Purchase expenditure equals price times quantity: $5 × 30 = $150. Storage costs and future sale proceeds are separate.

questions.prompt: How does a profit-maximizing cartel select total output?
options: Choose the quantity where marginal revenue equals marginal cost.
Choose the quantity where demand is zero.
Set marginal cost equal to average revenue at every quantity.
questions.explanation: At the profit-maximizing interior output, another unit adds as much revenue as cost.
questions.topic: Cartel output and incentives to cheat

questions.prompt: After selecting cartel output, where is its selling price read?
options: On the demand curve at that quantity.
questions.explanation: Demand shows the price buyers will pay for the chosen quantity. Marginal revenue is used to choose output, not to read the market price.
questions.topic: Cartel output and incentives to cheat

questions.prompt: Why might one producer secretly exceed its cartel quota?
options: At the cartel price, additional sales may yield revenue above the producer’s marginal cost.
Cheating always raises every member’s profit.
A quota makes additional production technologically impossible.
A cartel price must equal zero.
questions.explanation: The individual firm may benefit from extra output while others continue to restrict their sales.
questions.topic: Cartel output and incentives to cheat

questions.prompt: If many members exceed quotas, what tends to happen to the cartel price?
options: It falls as total supply expands.
It cannot change under any circumstances.
questions.explanation: Extra supply undermines the scarcity that supports the cartel’s high price.
questions.topic: Cartel output and incentives to cheat

questions.prompt: Which condition makes cartel coordination more difficult?
options: Different costs and incentives across many producers.
No outside competitors and no substitutes.
A guaranteed ability to enforce every quota.
questions.explanation: Members with different costs may disagree about quotas, and more participants make enforcement harder.
questions.topic: Cartel output and incentives to cheat

questions.prompt: How does a downturn often affect cartel discipline?
options: It increases pressure on members to cut prices or seek additional sales.
It abolishes all differences in costs.
questions.explanation: Falling demand and profits make members more tempted to win sales at others’ expense.
questions.topic: Cartel output and incentives to cheat

questions.prompt: What is trade creation in a customs union?
options: Lower-cost partner imports replace more expensive domestic production.
Higher-cost partner imports replace lower-cost outsider imports.
The government increases tariffs on every partner.
questions.explanation: Trade creation saves resources previously used in costly home production and can expand consumption.

questions.prompt: What is trade diversion?
options: Imports switch from a lower-cost outsider to a higher-cost member because of preferential treatment.
All countries switch to the world’s cheapest supplier.
Domestic output replaces cheaper imports without a policy change.
questions.explanation: The preference can make a member look cheaper after tariffs even when the outsider has lower underlying production costs.

questions.prompt: What is the basic welfare test for the union in this diagram?
options: Compare trade creation gains with trade diversion losses.
Count only the increase in imports.
Count only the fall in consumer prices.
Assume every trade agreement must improve welfare.
questions.explanation: A lower consumer price is not sufficient: lost tariff revenue and switching to a more costly supplier also matter.

questions.prompt: Suppose the two creation triangles are worth $8 and $5, while diversion costs $10. What is the net welfare change?
questions.explanation: Net welfare = 8 + 5 − 10 = +3. These illustrative areas apply the slide’s welfare method.

questions.prompt: For a triangle with a price change of $2 and a quantity change of 4, what is its area?
questions.explanation: A triangle’s area is one half × height × base: 0.5 × $2 × 4 = $4.

questions.prompt: A partner costs $30 per unit and an outsider $20. The outsider faces a $15 tariff while the partner pays none. Who supplies imports, assuming unlimited supply at these prices?
options: The partner, because its $30 delivered price is below the outsider’s $35.
The outsider, because its tariff-inclusive price is $20.
questions.explanation: Compare buyer prices after tariffs. The partner wins despite using $10 more resources per unit, illustrating diversion.

questions.prompt: How is a variable import levy set when the world price is below the support price?
options: World price divided by domestic demand.
questions.explanation: The levy fills the gap between the cheaper imported product and the supported domestic price.

questions.prompt: Using the slide’s $4.50 support price and $3.50 world price, what levy is needed?
If the world price falls to $2.50 while support remains $4.50, what happens to the levy?
questions.explanation: The new gap is $4.50 − $2.50 = $2.00. The levy rises as the world price falls.

questions.prompt: In the simple model, why does a foreign price cut fail to lower the protected domestic price?
options: The variable levy increases to offset the price cut.
The world price has no definition.
Foreign firms receive the levy revenue.
questions.explanation: A variable levy is adjusted to preserve the support price, unlike a fixed amount tariff.

questions.prompt: At the supported price, how do you find import quantity?
options: Subtract domestic quantity supplied from domestic quantity demanded.
Divide support price by world price.
questions.explanation: Imports fill the gap between what consumers want and what home producers supply at that price.

questions.prompt: Who generally gains from maintaining the higher domestic support price in this diagram?
options: Protected domestic producers, while domestic buyers pay more.
All domestic consumers without any cost.
Foreign producers who can undercut without limit.
questions.explanation: Higher prices support domestic production but raise the price consumers pay. National welfare needs a broader calculation.

questions.prompt: What does the vertical axis in the exporting-versus-investment diagram measure?
questions.explanation: The diagram compares average production costs, which are total costs divided by units produced.

questions.prompt: Why can exports from an existing large plant be attractive when the foreign market is small?
options: The existing plant may already exploit scale economies, avoiding a small high-cost foreign operation.
Small foreign plants necessarily have lower unit costs.
questions.explanation: A new plant serving only a small market may spread its fixed costs over too few units.

questions.prompt: How can growing foreign demand change the choice?
options: It can make local production more competitive by spreading fixed costs over more units.
It always makes local production impossible.
It eliminates every transport cost by definition.
It guarantees that licensing and exporting have identical risks.
questions.explanation: A larger local market can allow the foreign plant to move down its average-cost curve.

questions.prompt: What must be added to home production costs when comparing exports with local production?
options: Transport costs and applicable trade barriers, among other delivered costs.
Nothing; factory costs always equal delivered costs.
questions.explanation: The relevant comparison is the cost of serving customers, not just the cost at the factory gate.

questions.prompt: What can a high import tariff do to the location decision?
options: Make producing inside the foreign market more attractive than exporting into it.
Eliminate fixed costs of every domestic firm.
Force every investor to choose licensing only.
questions.explanation: Producing locally can avoid the tariff on the finished import, subject to other costs and rules.

questions.prompt: Does this cost diagram establish that foreign investment is always preferable?
options: No; the ranking depends on scale, delivered costs, and other conditions.
Yes; every foreign plant has zero cost.
Yes; demand and transport costs never matter.
questions.explanation: The diagram is a framework for comparing alternatives, not a universal ranking.

questions.prompt: What tradeoff can make licensing attractive in a small market?
options: It can avoid the fixed costs of establishing an owned foreign subsidiary.
Licensing necessarily has zero production cost.
The subsidiary never incurs fixed costs.
Licensing always gives the parent complete operational control.
questions.explanation: Setting up and managing a subsidiary may not be worthwhile at low sales volumes.

questions.prompt: What can favor an owned subsidiary as sales become large?
options: Lower variable costs can outweigh its fixed costs.
Fixed costs increase per unit without limit.
Large markets eliminate all control benefits.
The parent is forbidden to produce.
questions.explanation: Fixed cost per unit falls as output rises, allowing lower operating costs to become more important.

questions.prompt: What does the crossing point E represent in the lecture’s cost comparison?
options: The output where the two depicted alternatives have equal unit costs.
The output where both firms have zero revenue.
The maximum number of countries in a trade agreement.
questions.explanation: At a crossing, the curves have the same vertical value at the same quantity.

questions.prompt: Holding total fixed cost constant, what happens to average fixed cost as output rises?
options: It stays equal to marginal revenue.
questions.explanation: Average fixed cost = fixed cost / output. Dividing the same fixed amount by more units gives a smaller cost per unit.

questions.prompt: What important consideration is not fully captured by a simple cost-curve comparison?
options: Control of technology and exposure of know-how to a licensee.
The quantity on the horizontal axis.
The costs plotted on the vertical axis.
The location of the crossing point.
questions.explanation: Licensing may create risks involving intellectual property, quality control, and future competitors.

questions.prompt: A subsidiary has unit cost $8 and licensing $10 at the planned output. On cost grounds alone, which is preferred?
questions.explanation: Compare unit costs at the same output. The subsidiary is $2 cheaper per unit; other risks still need separate consideration.

questions.prompt: Why might a joint venture between existing competitors reduce welfare?
options: It can weaken competition, raise price, and restrict output.
It necessarily creates unlimited new competitors.
It always eliminates all production costs.
It makes demand perfectly elastic automatically.
questions.explanation: Combining rivals can increase market power. Reduced output can destroy mutually beneficial trades.
questions.topic: Joint ventures: efficiency and market power

questions.prompt: What can offset that market-power loss?
options: Sufficient reductions in real production costs.
A transfer of money with no resource savings, by itself.
Lower output with unchanged costs, by itself.
questions.explanation: Efficiency gains save resources. A large enough saving can offset the welfare cost of less competition.
questions.topic: Joint ventures: efficiency and market power

questions.prompt: Is a transfer from consumers to the firm automatically a net loss of total surplus?
options: No; distinguish a transfer from a deadweight loss.
Yes; every transfer destroys the same amount of resources.
No; transfers mean consumers cannot lose.
Yes; producer surplus is never counted.
questions.explanation: A transfer changes who receives surplus. Deadweight loss is surplus that disappears rather than moving between groups.
questions.topic: Joint ventures: efficiency and market power

questions.prompt: Suppose efficiency gains are $20 and lost gains from restricted output are $12. What is the net welfare effect?
questions.explanation: Net effect = real efficiency gains − welfare loss = 20 − 12 = +8.
questions.topic: Joint ventures: efficiency and market power

questions.prompt: With no cost reduction, what is the usual effect of replacing competition with monopoly in this model?
options: Higher price, lower output, and lower total surplus.
Lower price and higher output automatically.
questions.explanation: Without an offsetting efficiency gain, monopoly restricts output relative to the competitive benchmark.
questions.topic: Joint ventures: efficiency and market power

questions.prompt: Which conclusion is appropriate before calculating the areas?
options: The net welfare result is ambiguous until efficiency gains and market-power losses are compared.
Every joint venture must improve welfare.
Every joint venture must reduce welfare even with major cost savings.
questions.explanation: Both forces are possible. Their relative magnitudes determine the outcome.
questions.topic: Joint ventures: efficiency and market power

questions.prompt: What happens to U.S. labor supply when workers migrate from Mexico to the United States?
questions.explanation: Immigration increases the number of workers available at a given wage in the destination.

questions.prompt: Holding labor demand fixed, what happens to the wage in the destination?
options: It falls in this simple model.
It becomes zero in every case.
questions.explanation: A rightward supply shift moves the intersection down along labor demand. This is the diagram’s simplified assumption, not every real-world channel.

questions.prompt: What happens to labor supply and the wage in the origin country?
options: Supply shifts left and the wage rises, holding demand fixed.
Supply shifts right and the wage falls.
Supply and the wage both become zero.
Supply stays fixed and demand disappears.
questions.explanation: Emigration reduces the origin’s available labor. Its remaining workers become relatively scarcer.

questions.prompt: Who tends to gain in the destination in the lecture’s model?
options: Owners of capital, while competing native workers may lose.
Every native worker necessarily gains equally.
Only capital owners in the origin.
No one can gain from migration.
questions.explanation: More labor lowers wages and raises the income accruing to complementary capital in this model.

questions.prompt: How is the total wage bill calculated at an equilibrium?
options: Wage multiplied by the number of workers employed.
The area above labor demand only.
questions.explanation: The wage bill is a rectangle: each worker’s wage times the number of employed workers.

questions.prompt: Why can world output rise when labor moves between countries?
options: Workers move from a lower marginal product to a higher marginal product until the gap narrows.
Moving people creates output without work.
The origin loses no output when workers leave.
The destination always gains exactly what the origin loses.
questions.explanation: The destination’s extra production can exceed the origin’s lost production. The difference is the global efficiency gain in the model.

notes: Lower prices expand consumption and reduce costly domestic production: the two trade creation triangles.

notes: The levy equals the support price minus the world price, while the world price is below the support price.

graphs.title: Exporting or producing abroad
notes: Average cost means cost per unit. Compare full delivered costs at the expected sales volume.

notes: Combining competitors may raise market power. Lower costs may partly or fully offset this loss.

notes: Workers move toward higher wages. Immigration shifts destination labor supply right; emigration shifts origin labor supply left.
The wage bill is wage times workers. Capital income is the area below labor demand and above the wage.
Destination workers may lose while destination capital gains. In the origin, remaining workers may gain while capital loses.
World output rises in this model when labor moves to a higher marginal product. Migrants’ gains are distinct from gains to native workers.
